1.title: After the Death of Joshua
1.context: Judges opens where Joshua ended, with the tribes asking who will fight first. Adoni-bezek's punishment mirrors his own treatment of seventy kings, a detail the text lets him state himself.
1.question: When leadership changes hands, what do you ask God first?

1.title: Jerusalem Burned, and Caleb's Family Again
1.context: Judges retells Caleb's capture of Hebron and Othniel's winning of Achsah from Joshua 15, because Othniel is about to become the first judge. The same events stand in both books.
1.question: Why do you think the book repeats a story you have already read?

1.title: Iron Chariots, and the Jebusites Remain
1.context: Judah burns Jerusalem in verse 8, yet the Jebusites still live there in verse 21, because the city lay in Benjamin's allotment. A captured city and a kept city were different things.
1.question: What is the difference between winning a victory and keeping it?

1.title: The Catalog of Failures
1.context: Chapter 1 ends as a list: tribe after tribe settles for forced labor instead of driving out the inhabitants. Dan is the only tribe shown losing ground, pushed into the hills by the Amorites.
1.question: Where does compromise usually begin in your experience, with a decision or with a drift?

1.title: The Angel at Bochim
1.context: Bochim means weeping. The angel's charge repeats warnings Joshua gave before his death, including the image of thorns and a snare from Joshua 23:13.
1.question: When have you grieved over a pattern without yet changing it?

1.title: Another Generation Rose Up
1.context: Judges buries Joshua a second time. His burial town is spelled Timnath-heres here and Timnath-serah in Joshua 24:30, a small variation between the two books' records.
1.question: What carries faith from one generation to the next, and what happens when it is only inherited?

1.title: The Turn, the Consequence, the Rescue
1.context: The Baals and Ashtoreths were the gods of the peoples Israel now lived among, tied to rain, harvests, and ordinary survival. The text says the LORD was moved to pity by Israel's groaning under its oppressors.
1.question: Which stage of the cycle do you find easiest to recognize in your own life?

1.title: The Relapse, and the Test
1.context: Each relapse is described as worse than the fathers before it. The nations that remain are reframed as a test of whether Israel will keep the way of the LORD as their fathers did.
1.question: What would it look like for a pattern to end one turn lower every time, and what interrupts it?

2.title: Left to Test Israel, and the First Judge
2.context: The nations left in the land are named as a test. Othniel, Caleb's nephew and son-in-law, is the first judge, and his short account sets the pattern the others will be measured against.
2.question: What does a clean, faithful response look like before things get complicated?

2.title: Eighteen Years Under Eglon
2.context: Moab, Ammon, and Amalek together held even Jericho, called the City of Palms. Ehud's short sword hung on his right thigh because guards checked the left side, where right-handed men wore theirs.
2.question: Why might God choose a deliverer whose difference is the very thing others overlook?

2.title: The Secret Message
2.context: Ehud turns back at the idols near Gilgal, the place of the memorial stones. Eglon rises to receive a word from God, and the locked doors of the cool upper room buy the assassin his escape.
2.question: What details in this story stand out to you as the narrator's way of slowing you down?

2.title: The Fords Seized, and Shamgar's Oxgoad
2.context: Seizing the Jordan fords cut off the Moabites' retreat, the same crossings Israel once used to enter the land. Shamgar gets one verse and a farmer's oxgoad, and the text still says he saved Israel.
2.question: What small or unlikely thing has God used in your life?

3.title: Twenty Years of Iron
3.context: Hazor, burned by Joshua, is again a Canaanite capital under another Jabin. Deborah is the only judge in the book shown settling disputes, sitting under her palm tree between Ramah and Bethel.
3.question: What does it say that Israel's deliverer was already serving faithfully before any crisis came?

3.title: Barak's Condition
3.context: Barak would go only if Deborah went with him. Deborah agrees and tells him the honor for Sisera's fall will go to a woman. Readers have debated Barak's faith ever since; the text states his condition and its price without a verdict.
3.question: When is asking for support a strength, and when does it cost you something?

3.title: The Day the LORD Routed Sisera
3.context: Nine hundred iron chariots needed flat, dry ground. Heber the Kenite's tent near Kedesh is planted in the story one verse before the battle, because it will matter within the hour.
3.question: When have the conditions you trusted most turned out to be the problem?

3.title: Jael and the Tent Peg
3.context: Jael was a Kenite, kin to Moses by marriage, living at peace with Jabin. Tent pegs and hammers were her everyday tools as a tent-dwelling woman. The honor Deborah promised to a woman lands on her, not on Deborah.
3.question: What surprises you most about where this victory was completed?

3.title: The Song: Rain, Muster, and Curse
3.context: Chapter 5 is Deborah and Barak's song, among the oldest poetry in the Bible. It credits the storm and the flooding Kishon, praises the tribes that came, and names the ones that stayed home.
3.question: How does singing about an event change what the event means?

3.title: The Window, and Forty Years of Rest
3.context: The song ends at a window, with Sisera's mother watching for a chariot that will never come. Prose gave the battle and the song gave its meaning, each keeping details the other does not.
3.question: Whose viewpoint in a familiar story have you never stopped to consider?

4.title: The Locust Years and the Prophet
4.context: Midian's raids were timed to the harvest and came from the east with innumerable camels. Before sending a deliverer, God sends a prophet whose whole message is a reminder and a charge: you did not obey.
4.question: Why might God answer a cry for help with a reminder first?

4.title: The Angel in the Winepress
4.context: Threshing was done on open windy floors; Gideon works in a winepress pit to stay hidden. His argument quotes the Exodus the way Israel's fathers told it, and God answers the man rather than the argument.
4.question: What question would you ask if you were standing in Gideon's winepress?

4.title: Fire on the Rock, and the Altar at Night
4.context: The offering consumed by fire from the rock repeats a pattern from earlier theophanies. Gideon's first assignment targets his own father's altar, and he does it at night because he is afraid, which the text states plainly.
4.question: What obedience have you done quietly because you were afraid to do it openly?

4.title: Jerubbaal, and the Fleece
4.context: Joash defends his son with a challenge: if Baal is a god, let him fight his own battle. The name Jerubbaal means let Baal contend. The fleece is asked twice, reversed the second time.
4.question: How do you tell the difference between seeking confirmation and stalling?

4.title: Thirty-Two Thousand Become Three Hundred
4.context: The law in Deuteronomy 20 already sent fearful soldiers home. The water test at the spring of Harod leaves three hundred, and God sends Gideon into the enemy camp at night to hear a dream about a loaf of barley bread.
4.question: What has God ever reduced in your life before He used it?

4.title: Horns, Jars, and the Heads of Princes
4.context: The middle watch began around ten at night. Three hundred torches and horns convinced a vast camp it was surrounded, and the Midianites turned their swords on each other. Oreb and Zeeb mean raven and wolf.
4.question: When have you seen a battle won mainly by standing in the place you were given?

5.title: Gleanings of Ephraim, and Bread Refused
5.context: Ephraim's complaint after the battle repeats a pattern that will return with Jephthah. Gideon's answer gives Ephraim the honor of capturing the princes. Succoth and Penuel, east of the Jordan, refuse bread to his exhausted men.
5.question: When is a soft answer wisdom, and when does the same person stop giving soft answers?

5.title: The Kings Taken, and Israel Punished
5.context: Of a hundred and thirty-five thousand eastern swordsmen, fifteen thousand remained at Karkor. Gideon disciplines Succoth with thorns and pulls down Penuel's tower, the deliverer now punishing Israelite towns.
5.question: Where do you see victory starting to change Gideon?

5.title: The Crown Refused, the Ephod Built
5.context: An ephod was a priestly garment; Gideon's golden one became an object of worship at Ophrah. He refuses the crown in words, then takes a royal household, seventy sons, and a son named Abimelech, which means my father is king.
5.question: Can you refuse something in words while accepting it in practice?

5.title: One Stone, and a Parable from Gerizim
5.context: Shechem's leaders fund Abimelech with seventy shekels from the temple of Baal-berith. Jotham's parable of the trees is the Bible's first fable, spoken from Mount Gerizim, the mountain of blessing in Deuteronomy 27 and Joshua 8.
5.question: What does Jotham's parable say about the kind of leader who most wants the job?

5.title: Fire Begins to Move
5.context: The text says God sent a spirit of animosity between Abimelech and Shechem so that the murder of the seventy brothers would be answered. Gaal's revolt is talked up at a harvest festival in the house of their god.
5.question: How do the early warnings of a judgment differ from the judgment itself?

5.title: The Tower, the Millstone, and the Audit
5.context: Sowing a captured city with salt cursed it against future crops. At Thebez an unnamed woman drops an upper millstone, and the narrator closes Abimelech's account by stating plainly that God repaid the wickedness of both sides.
5.question: What do you make of the fact that the book gives Abimelech no title of judge at all?

6.title: Quiet Judges, Then the Whole Pantheon
6.context: Tola and Jair together judge forty-five years with no war recorded. The relapse that follows names seven directions of idolatry at once, from the Baals to the gods of the Philistines.
6.question: What do long quiet seasons protect, and what can they hide?

6.title: Go Cry to the Gods You Chose
6.context: This is the only time in the book God answers the cry with a refusal first. Israel responds by putting away the foreign gods before any deliverer appears, and the text says He could no longer bear their misery.
6.question: What is the difference between confessing with words and putting something away?

6.title: The Outcast Fetched Home
6.context: Jephthah, driven out by his brothers because of his mother, leads a band in the land of Tob. The elders who fetch him swear their oath with the LORD as witness at Mizpah.
6.question: Have you ever needed help from someone you once pushed away, or been that person for someone else?

6.title: A Statesman's Brief, and a Blank Check
6.context: Jephthah's message to Ammon recounts three hundred years of history and cites Sihon's defeat and Balak's restraint. The vow follows the Spirit's coming upon him, and its wording leaves the greeter to whoever comes out the door first.
6.question: What makes a promise to God careful, and what makes one reckless?

6.title: Tambourines at the Door
6.context: Women greeting a returning victor with tambourines and dancing was Israel's custom since Miriam at the sea. Jephthah's daughter asks for two months to mourn her virginity, and Israel's young women kept four days a year in her memory.
6.question: The text does not praise or condemn what happened in so many words. How do you read its silence?

6.title: Shibboleth at the Fords
6.context: Ephraim's dialect dropped the first sound of the word shibboleth, which means a stream or an ear of grain. Forty-two thousand died at the crossings where Ehud once won a victory for all Israel.
6.question: What small differences between people get treated as matters of life and death?

7.title: A Nazirite from the Womb
7.context: For the first time the text records no cry from Israel, only forty years of Philistine rule. A Nazirite's vow, from Numbers 6, meant no grape products, no razor, and no contact with the dead. Manoah's wife reasons more clearly than Manoah when the angel ascends in the flame.
7.question: What do you notice about who receives the announcement, and who has to catch up?

7.title: Get Her for Me
7.context: The narrator says plainly that Samson's demand for a Philistine wife was an occasion God was seeking against the Philistines. On the road Samson tears a lion apart and later eats honey from its carcass, a Nazirite handling the dead in secret.
7.question: How do you hold together Samson's calling and Samson's choices in these verses?

7.title: The Riddle and the Tears
7.context: A wedding feast ran seven days, and the thirty companions were assigned to the bridegroom. The riddle is unwinnable because it rests on a secret no one witnessed, so the companions threaten Samson's wife with the fire her cooperation was meant to escape.
7.question: When has pressure from people you love worn down a boundary you meant to keep?

7.title: The Wager Paid in Blood, and the Foxes
7.context: Samson pays the riddle debt with the clothes of thirty men killed at Ashkelon. The foxes, tied tail to tail with torches, burn the Philistines' grain, vineyards, and olive groves at harvest.
7.question: How does the back-and-forth of revenge keep each side convinced it is only answering the other?

7.title: Bound by His Own Tribe, Freed at Lehi
7.context: Three thousand men of Judah arrest Samson rather than join him, the measure of forty years under Philistine rule. His song over the jawbone plays on the Hebrew words for donkey and heap, and God answers his thirst at En-hakkore.
7.question: What does it cost a person to be delivered by someone their own people will not stand with?

8.title: The Gates of Gaza, and the Valley of Sorek
8.context: Gaza was the southernmost of the Philistines' five cities, each ruled by a lord. The five lords together offer Delilah fifty-five hundred shekels of silver, eleven hundred each, for the secret of Samson's strength.
8.question: What does Samson seem unable to do, even when he knows a place or a person is dangerous?

8.title: All That Was in His Heart
8.context: Delilah's fourth approach uses love itself as the argument. The text says she pressed him daily until he was sick to death, and that when he slept, he did not know the LORD had departed from him.
8.question: Where do you see the difference between Samson's strength and the presence that gave it?

8.title: The Mill, and the Feast of Dagon
8.context: Grinding grain was household labor, now done by the blinded deliverer in a Gaza prison. The Philistine lords read his capture as Dagon's victory and hold a great sacrifice, while the text quietly notes his hair growing back.
8.question: What do you do with the small signs of hope in a season that looks finished?

8.title: Between the Pillars
8.context: The temple held all five lords and about three thousand people on the roof. Samson's second recorded prayer asks for strength once more and names its motive: vengeance for his two eyes.
8.question: How do you pray honestly when your motives are mixed?

8.title: Buried Between Zorah and Eshtaol
8.context: His family buries him in his father Manoah's tomb, in the same ground where the Spirit first began to stir him. The book's verdict is measured: he killed more in his death than in his life, and the deliverance he began stayed unfinished.
8.question: What part of Samson's story do you find hardest to settle in your mind?

9.title: Dedicated to the LORD, for an Idol
9.context: The silver Micah's mother dedicates was stolen by Micah himself, and two hundred of the eleven hundred shekels become a graven image. He staffs his private shrine first with his son, then with a wandering Levite hired for ten shekels a year, clothes, and food.
9.question: What arrangements have you seen that look like devotion but are really control?

9.title: Dan Looks North
9.context: Dan's spies lodge at Micah's house and receive an oracle from his hired priest. Laish, modeled on Sidon, lives quiet and unsuspecting in the far north, far from any ally. The spies' report borrows the language of Caleb's good report.
9.question: When is confidence in God's promise being used to cover a plan God never gave?

9.title: The Shrine Stolen
9.context: Six hundred armed Danites stand at the gate while five men carry out the shrine. The priest trades up from one household to a tribe, and Micah's cry names his religion exactly: you took the gods I had made.
9.question: What does Micah's loss show about things we make and then depend on?

9.title: Dan, and the Grandson of Moses
9.context: The priest is named only at the end: Jonathan son of Gershom, the son of Moses. His family serves Dan's idol until the captivity of the land, centuries later, while God's house stands at Shiloh the whole time.
9.question: What does it mean that a legacy can be carried by name and lost in practice?

10.title: We Will Go On to Gibeah
10.context: The Levite's father-in-law delays the journey with hospitality for five days, so the party reaches Gibeah in Benjamin after dark instead of stopping at Jebus, which is Jerusalem. No one in Gibeah offers them a home for the night.
10.question: How do small delays and assumptions combine to put people in danger?

10.title: The Doorway, and Twelve Pieces
10.context: An old man, himself a sojourner from Ephraim, takes the travelers in. The mob's demand and the host's counter-offer echo Genesis 19 at Sodom, this time in an Israelite city. The woman is found at dawn with her hands on the threshold.
10.question: The text tells this without decorating it. What do you think the narrator wants Israel, and you, to feel about Gibeah?

10.title: As One Man, Defeat, and the Ambush
10.context: Israel assembles four hundred thousand men at Mizpah. The Levite's testimony omits his own part in sending the woman out. Benjamin's seven hundred left-handed slingers fulfill the description given of the tribe in this same book, and Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, still serves before the ark, marking how early in the era this war falls.
10.question: Why do you think God let Israel lose twice, at heavy cost, before giving the victory He promised?

10.title: Wives for the Survivors
10.context: Two oaths collide: no daughters to Benjamin, and death for whoever missed the assembly. Jabesh-gilead's four hundred young women and the arranged seizure at Shiloh's feast are Israel's loopholes, engineered by the elders so no one technically gives a daughter.
10.question: What happens when people treat the letter of a vow as more important than the people it crushes?

10.title: Everyone Did What Was Right in His Own Eyes
10.context: The book ends on its refrain, with no judge, king, or resolution. The next story in this series' order is Ruth, set in these same days of the judges, where the same land that produced Gibeah also produces a story of loyalty and kindness.
10.question: After all you have read in Judges, what do you make of its final sentence?
